name: Sterilise
summary: Clean first, then kill what’s left: dirt shields germs from heat, chlorine and light. Boiling handles most needs, and a pressure cooker at full pressure reaches the temperature hospitals sterilise at. Diluted bleach or pool chlorine disinfects surfaces and tools. UV-C lamps hide in pond clarifiers, air purifiers and water treatment units, but they burn eyes and skin.

parts.why: Bleach and pool chlorine disinfect surfaces and tools
UV-C lamps kill germs on surfaces and in water
Electric boiling and steaming where power allows
Fuel for boiling and pressure cooking

tips: Boiling tools for 10 minutes disinfects them but does not sterilise: disinfection is not sporicidal (CDC disinfection). Steam under pressure does sterilise (CDC disinfection): use a pressure cooker at full pressure for 15–30 minutes. These times are rules of thumb, not from a tested source.
Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other cleaners. It makes toxic gas.
Never look at a lit UV-C lamp, and keep skin out of its light.

Bleach weakens with age and heat. Clorox says it keeps up to a year in a cool, dry place out of the sun, then breaks down faster until it is too weak to disinfect (Clorox date). Don't guess a stronger mix for old bleach: use a fresh bottle.

Check chlorinated drinking water with a pool or spa test kit that reads free chlorine (a DPD kit). Aim for at least 0.5 mg/L after 30 minutes if the pH is below 8, or 1 mg/L after 60 minutes at pH 8 or above (WEDC Mobile Note 7, quoting WHO; MSF cholera). Smell alone is a rough check.

sources.title: WEDC Mobile Note 7: WEDC (Loughborough University), Mobile Note 7: Chlorination (quotes WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality, 2004, p. 194)
MSF cholera: Medecins Sans Frontieres, Management of a cholera epidemic (medical guidelines), 3.3 Supply of safe water
Clorox date: Clorox, How to tell when a bleach bottle was made
CDC disinfection: CDC, Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities, Introduction, Methods, Definition of Terms
